messages.body_plain:
Hi

We are using R for a course, and want students to send their homeworks in Rmd format. Ideally, the Rmd files could be sent by students to a centralised repository, kept inaccessible for a while (to prevent copying from others), then made accessible to all to present results during discussion section.

Which tool, workflow would you recommend? One possibility would be to ask students to send through Canvas, or Rpubs, then for us to centralize, and push into github or alike. That's the easiest on the student side, but can require quite a few manual steps on the TA side.

An alternative is for students to have their own github account, then do pull requests. This is more complicated on student side, and I am not sure how to handle the "undisclosed period", as ?

Any ides or suggestions for other worflows?

Thanks!

Matthieu

messages.body_plain:
Just to chime in, we are using github classrooms for an R course, which has been great, however, at the moment it's mainly been a one way usage. We create a repository which Github Classroom then uses to create a repository for each student, appending their username to the repo name. I don't think it is currently functional for folks to submit things back in the way that you are describing (without some significant overhead burden on the student and instructors...branching, merge/merge conflicts, pull requests, general mayhem).

That being said, any reason not to submit content via a google form? You can now attach files via a google form, which could go into a folder that is only shared with TAs/instructors. After you've reviewed the Rmd's, you could move the files to a new shared folder on Google Drive which the entire class would have access to. The google form would allow you to track who submits what and when, ensuring that submissions happen by a specific deadline. That also eliminates the need for folks to need to know Git (unless that's a component you are planning on teaching).  If not that, you could use Box in a similar way...we've had success doing this for submissions to a student magazine (see our submission form here <https://aggiebrickyard.github.io/submissions/> on the Aggie Brickyard site

Good luck.

Ryan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaime, Michael and Ryan

Thanks for the inputs! To answer first the few questions, students are expected to have little to no knowledge of R and git(hub), but that's first year PhD class. And yes, the idea of Rpubs was that you would need to know the colleagues pseudo to access their files, so not the most secure indeed.

The github classroom tool seems interesting. Do I understand well that it sets up ready github repos for the students (who still need to create github accounts)? Which automatically will push to a repository we control? That seems pretty nice. We could have that repo private (though that costs a few $), and eventually push later on to a public git repo, so that everyone can see everyone's homeworks. That's the two steps we need, we don't need a push-back system actually.

But otherwise, yes we could simply ask to use the Canvas assignment system, which seems indeed to be bulk downloadable. Then have a simple script compiling the Rmd, and pushing these to a pubic github repo, might be the easiest.

Thanks for the valuable comments!

Matthieu

Hi Folks,

No work session as it's Martin Luther King Jr. Day tomorrow (a holiday). We'll reconvene next week at the DSI.

In honor of the holiday (and speeches lacking profanity), here's a figure showing the most commonly used words in MLK's "I Have a Dream <https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gge-ucd/R-DAVIS/master/data/I_have_a_dream_1963.md>" speech (and some code below).

Adios,
Ryan

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(readr);
  library(ggplot2)
})

# read in the data (same as you would a csv)
mlk<-read_lines("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gge-ucd/R-DAVIS/master/data/I_have_a_dream_1963.md")

# this splits the chunk of text into lines
mlk_text <- data_frame(line = 1:length(mlk), text = mlk)

# filter blank lines (even rows)
mlk_text <- mlk_text %>% filter(line %% 2 == 1) %>%
  mutate(line = 1:nrow(.)) # renumber lines

# Make single word vector
mlk_text<- mlk_text %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, text)

# Now remove all the stop words using an "anti_join"
tidy_mlk <- mlk_text %>%
  anti_join(stop_words)
# count use and then plot by most to least for words used more than twice in the speech
tidy_mlk %>%
  count(word, sort = TRUE) %>%
  filter(n > 2) %>%
  mutate(word = reorder(word, n)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(word, n)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill="forestgreen") +
  xlab(NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  coord_flip() + labs(x="Words used more than 2x", title="I Have A Dream Speech, MLK Jr. (1963)")
--

Judging from the example data at: http://swat.tamu.edu/software/links/, the files are simple fixed-width/space separated formatted files with a header section. The two tricks are:

1) find the start of the table: you can do this with readLines and then grep to find the column names

2) read in the table with read.table

For the example output file attached, this is sufficient:

txt= readLines("output.hru")
i = grep("LULC",txt)[1]
df = read.table("output.hru",skip= i)

If the file is different than this one, attach it.

Hi, Hannah.  I haven't used Overleaf (but I can see some use for it among some people I work with).  And I've personally used knitr/rmarkdown only to produce documents for my colleagues.  I can't comment as to how it might interface to, say, stylesheets for a given journal.  But I do note that it's possible to include LaTeX packages -- as well as LaTeX code, of course -- in Rmd documents.  See the appended for a slightly-edited example of the YAML section of one of my Rmd documents.

Regarding the motivation for my suggestion: I just have the impression that the knitr/rmarkdown stuff is being actively developed by the RStudio folks.  If improvements are going to appear, it seems likely that they will appear first (only?) in knitr/rmarkdown.  You can see the advertising copy at:

    http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/

and I now discover that there are formats for some journals:

    http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/formats.html

-- Mike

---
title: blah, blah
author:
fontsize: 12pt
output:

- \lfoot{\textbf{Johd Doe}}

- \rfoot{\thepage}

Hi all,

A few thoughts. Great suggestion for a workshop, however, I'm not sure the D-RUG is the best place to have a LaTeX talk (unless we have a volunteer willing!). But, a recent UC Davis grad, Brendan Barrett gave a great tutorial on using LaTeX and overleaf last quarter. The video is here <https://youtu.be/5dnK2knSu0Q>, and the overleaf file is here <https://www.overleaf.com/read/vtksfyhbcthw>.

Having said that, as Michael mentions, RMarkdown is really an amazing and excellent platform that can be used to write manuscripts <http://svmiller.com/blog/2016/02/svm-r-markdown-manuscript/> (see here <http://rmhogervorst.nl/cleancode/blog/2017/03/14/writing-manuscripts-in-rstudio.html> and here <https://libscie.github.io/rmarkdown-workshop/handout.html> too), dissertations <https://github.com/ismayc/thesisdown> (even a UCD version which is only in Markdown <https://github.com/davharris/Davis-dissertation-template>), etc. I'm currently using it for a manuscript and it's been great thus far.

I think there are lots of options to integrate RMarkdown and LaTeX.  Here's a few additional things folks might find useful:
A recent package called TinyTeX <https://yihui.name/tinytex/> (written by the same person who wrote the knitr, bookdown, and xaringan packages, all worth checking out) is a nice way to get LaTeX installed on your machine via R.
For citations, there is a great add in called citr <https://github.com/crsh/citr>, which makes it easy to add citations to a RMarkdown or markdown file. You can add a csl file for just about any journal of your choosing (see this RStudio help page on bibliographies and citations <http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com/authoring_bibliographies_and_citations.html>) and it will format the citations automatically.
Hope this is useful.

Adios,
Ryan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hannah

Adding a few thought to the topic. First of all, knitr is not only about markdown, but also LaTeX. So in general you would not use Sweave anymore, but knitr instead, then choose whether you want to type in markdown or LaTeX. It's a little confusing in Rstudio, as to write in TeX using knitr you would go create an R Sweave document (link <https://support.rstudio.com/hc/en-us/articles/200552056-Using-Sweave-and-knitr>)!

To choose between LaTeX and markdown, I would take these elements into account:

trade-off ease/complexity: either easy syntax for simple documents, or complicated syntax for very sophisticated documents.
publication-wise: which output is expected for the journals in your field? I am not aware of many journals accepting html manuscripts. There are a bunch of journals on the other side having LaTeX templates. But then markdown can also output in Word format, something most journals will accept...
tables in your paper: do you want to have fancy tables with regression output? Which R package will you use to create these tables? xtable? texreg? stargazer? Some of them output both in html or TeX, give it a try first?

Finally: there is the LyX software, a "Word-like" editor processing LaTeX underneath. Learning it will be even easier than learning the markdown syntax. And you run it with knitr too. That's very personal, but that's would be my favourite choice by far, helps you keeping a clean document while seeing the structure of your document immediately. So I would use this for my main paper, using knitr inside, together with tables exported in TeX format.

I am also happy to make a knitr/LaTeX presentation. I guess a TeX talk at RUG is as justified as... a markdown talk :-)

Matthieu

Hi, Bic.  I don't have an answer to your question, but I do have a
question about it.

First, I note that the `barplot` function does have arguments "col"
and "add".  These might (or might not) be of some use.

My question is, basically, what is your ultimate goal here?  It
appears that you're trying to compare *rows* of a data frame.  It
seems clear from your example that the different columns of the data
frame have very different scales (dpi of 2329.68 vs. ddpi of 2.81, for
instance).  I don't see the point of plotting them on the same plot.
Even if you can manage to constructively add all the various plots
together, the dpi column is always doing to dominate the picture,
making it hard to distinguish variations in pop75, for instance, even
if the different rows are color-coded.

It occurs to me that this could be made somewhat more meaningful by
normalizing each column to the max value in that column.  E.g.:

> (test["Australia", "pop75"] / max(test["pop75"]))
[1] 0.6478555
>

I.e., Australia's "pop75" is about 65% of the max.  Doing something
like this would at least make the scales the same for all columns.

-- Mike

PERMANOVA and MANOVA can be used in pretty much the same way, but the assumptions of PERMANOVA are not as strict, so can be used if the data are not perfectly normal.

What does your code look like so far? If you are willing to share a sample of your data I might be able to be more help.

Since you have multiple levels of nesting in your design, you want to constrain the permutations of your PerMANOVA using the "how" funciton. It sounds like the formula you are trying to set up should look something like this:

h1 <- how(within = Within(type = "series"), plots = Plots(strata = subplots, type = "series"), blocks = mainplot)
adonis(diversitymatrix ~ N + C/N + pH, strata = plot, method = h1)

See if this explanation helps at all.

Hey people,

I have been messing around with combn() and mutate_all() and all sort of other stuff trying to get something to work. I'd like to be able to mutate a dataframe I have, creating a new column for all combinations of paired columns. If there's a value > 0 in both of those columns, TRUE,  if < 0, FALSE (in my real data set the values may be higher than 1, but I just care if they're >0).

I have been able to implement a toy version of it (below). However, in my real data there's 78 possible combinations of columns, and I really don't want to have to do each one individually, plus that would be error prone.

The transmute() part is where I'd want to be able to also use combn() or some other function rather than manually typing out each new variable name. The remaining stuff (mutate >>> summarise) is just for setting up what I'll do with the data next. Bonus points if you show me how to transmute and preserve the "familyID" column.

Help?

require(tidyverse)

site01 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site02 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site03 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)

              site01site03 = if_else(site01>0 & site03>0, T, F),

  mutate(familyID=familyID) %>%
  gather(site_combo, num_true, -familyID) %>%
  group_by(site_combo) %>%
  summarise(connections = sum(num_true))

Thank you!!

So not sure I'm 100% positive I understand what you're looking for, but I think it's something like this. I basically use crossing() to build out all combinations, remove the like combinations (site01 to site01) using filter(), and then do two full_joins to the two sites in the comparisons (A and B). I do this on nested dataframes per familyID because that way you can preserve it. Be cautious with the function I wrote; dplyr/tidyverse uses non-standard evaluation and I don't quote anything here, but should be fine-ish.

set.seed(0)

familyID = sample(letters, 5, replace = FALSE)
site01 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site02 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site03 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)

dd <- df %>% gather(site, value, site01:site03)
all_sites <- unique(dd$site)

expand_join <- function(x, .sites) {
 crossing(site_a = .sites, site_b = .sites) %>%
   # join with the original sites to A in pair and B in pair
   full_join(x, by=c('site_a'='site')) %>% full_join(x, by=c('site_b'='site')) %>%
   # filter out both same site comparisons
    filter(site_a != site_b) %>%
   # create a 'both' column when both eval to TRUE, and clean up the data, and spread it out
    mutate(both= value.x & value.y) %>% select(-value.x, -value.y) %>% unite('site_pair', site_a, site_b) %>% spread(site_pair, both)
}

# I think it's safer to use nested list cols. We could do it likely in a complicated join, but that'd be fragile.
dd %>% group_by(familyID) %>% nest() %>% mutate(comp = map(data, expand_join, .sites=all_sites)) %>% unnest(comp)

library(tidyverse)

#function to get the combinations
# from:  # https://stackoverflow.com/questions/17171148/non-redundant-version-of-expand-grid
expand.grid.unique <-
    function(x, y, include.equals=FALSE) {
        x <- unique(x)
        y <- unique(y)
        g <-
        function(i){
            z <- setdiff(y, x[seq_len(i-include.equals)])
            if(length(z)) cbind(x[i], z, deparse.level=0)
        }
        do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(x), g))
    }

#make the site names
site_names <- paste0("site0", c(1:3), sep= "")

#make the frame of combinations and combo-names
name_frame <-
    expand.grid.unique(site_names, site_names) %>%
        as_tibble() %>%
        rename(name1 = V1, name2 = V2) %>%
        mutate(namename = paste(name1, name2, sep= ""))

#make up fake data

familyID = sample(letters, 5, replace = FALSE)
site01 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site02 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)
site03 = sample(c(0,1), 5, replace=TRUE)

#this function takes the 3 names from the list and the dataframe (called df)
# and returns the named column with T/F
do_fun <-
    function(df, name1, name2, namename) {
        namename <- rlang::sym(namename)
        name1 <- rlang::sym(name1)
        name2 <- rlang::sym(name2)
        df %>%
            select(familyID, !!name1, !!name2) %>%
            transmute(!!namename := if_else(!!name1 > 0 & !!name2 > 0, T, F))

    mutate(familyID = df$familyID) %>%

Here is a bit of code I wrote yesterday using grid.arrange with a for loop. Ignore everything in the for loop, main point is that I have grid.arrange outside the for loop, and use do.call()

p <- list()
for (i in 1:length(codNames)) {
  pop <- datalist[[i]]
  pop <- pop[pop$AGE > 5,] # plot abundance at older ages to see contrast better
  pop <- pop[pop$YEAR %in% c('1965','1970','1975','1980','1985','1990','1995','2000','2005'),]
    # plot only a few years so it isn't as messy
  #pop$CANUM <- as.numeric(as.character(pop$CANUM)) # convert abundances to numeric
  #pop$YEAR <- as.numeric(as.character(pop$YEAR))
  #pop$YEAR <- factor(pop$YEAR)

  p[[i]] <- ggplot(data=pop, aes(x=AGE, y=CANUM, color=YEAR)) +
            geom_line() +
            theme(legend.position='none') +
            ggtitle(codNames[i]) +
            scale_colour_gradient2()
}
do.call(grid.arrange,p)
